howto.summary: Browse and search organizations and upcoming events, review official group pages, register for events, and join groups that match your interests.
howto.steps: Open Groups or Events; search or filter by interest/category; open the official page; join the group or register for the event.

howto.summary: Create an event from the group-management dashboard and enter the name, description, type, coordinator, date/time, and location.
howto.steps: Manage Group > Events > Create Event; complete What, When, and Where; then add GW-required registration, visibility, and approval information.

howto.summary: Update the logo, cover image, mission, membership benefits, constitution, officers, events, posts, news, photos, and visible sections.
howto.steps: Manage Group > Dashboard > Group Page; edit page settings and individual sections.

howto.summary: Add individual members or upload a member list and optionally notify them.
howto.steps: Manage Group > Members > Current Members > Add Member, or select Upload Members for a bulk list.

howto.summary: Add an existing member as an officer and assign the appropriate position.
howto.steps: Manage Group > Dashboard > Officers > Add Officer; find the member and assign a position.

howto.summary: Send targeted emails or newsletters, use notifications, and review open/click data. Events can also be shared through email, social media, chat, and mobile notifications.
howto.steps: Choose a specific audience; write one clear call to action; test the message; send it; review opens, clicks, registrations, and attendance.

howto.summary: Authorized event managers can use QR codes, student IDs, manual entry, computers, or the mobile app to record attendance.
howto.steps: Open event check-in tools; choose an approved method; check in attendees; review the attendance report; follow up afterward.

howto.summary: Create forms and surveys, set access and dates, notify officers, collect responses, and run elections.
howto.steps: Manage Group > Forms/Surveys; create the form; set access, dates, notifications, and privacy; use the Election question type for elections.

groups.description: The mission of the American Medical Physiology Club is to foster an inclusive and interdisciplinary pre-health community at the George Washington University in which students can grow academically, professionally, and personally. AMPC strives to make the pre-health experience more collaborative and accessible by connecting students with peers, mentors, healthcare professionals, researchers, and meaningful opportunities to explore the diverse careers available within healthcare. Through education, mentorship, service, professional development, and community-building, AMPC empowers students to explore their interests and prepare for future careers in healthcare. The American Medical Physiology Club (AMPC) provides GW students with opportunities to explore healthcare careers, develop pre-professional skills, gain meaningful experience, and connect with a supportive community of fellow pre-health students. Members have access to healthcare career panels and professional workshops, hands-on clinical and skills-based events, research opportunities, shadowing connections, mentorship, community service, academic and professional development resources, and social events. Through partnerships with healthcare professionals, researchers, faculty, and organizations throughout the D.C. area, AMPC helps members build the knowledge, experiences, and relationships that will support them throughout their pre-health journeys. Membership is completely free and open to all GW students! AMPC seeks to: Expose students to the diversity of careers, specialties, and pathways available within healthcare. Provide hands-on and experiential opportunities that allow members to develop practical clinical and pre-professional skills. Connect students with healthcare professionals, faculty, researchers, mentors, and other resources throughout GW and the greater D.C. community. Expand access to research, shadowing, service, mentorship, and professional development opportunities. Support members' academic and professional growth through workshops, guidance, and peer mentorship. Promote meaningful service and engagement with the surrounding community. Build an inclusive, supportive pre-health community that emphasizes collaboration rather than competition and encourages members to support one another throughout their undergraduate and professional journeys.

Furthermore, we are organizing a panel featuring various types of oncologists, including as medical, surgical, and radiation oncologists, to educate students about the full scope of oncology practice. Community Service Events/Volunteer : To continue with the partnerships we created last year, we plan to attend multiple community events this year, including the Race4Her and Miles for Melanoma 5k. Research: To improve oncology research opportunities for GW medical students will be partnering with the GW oncology faculty, Children's National Oncology Faculty and the DC VA hospital to connect interested students with research mentors. Additionally, we hope to participate in the ASCO Medical Student and Resident Abstract forums. We would also like to host practice presentations for students who are planning to present their research at local or national meetings.

groups.description: Asian American Student Association (AASA) is a student-led organization dedicated to educating our peers and community about the Asian American identity. This group was founded to create a safe and inclusive space for members and allies of our community. These spaces are intended for important conversations surrounding issues prevalent in the Asian American community. We aim to educate, advocate for, and empower our peers within GW. AASA is constantly looking to interrogate what it means to be Asian American as we understand that this label encompasses many identities and experiences. AASA does not look to define what it means to be Asian American but looks to create a space where students may discuss this question themselves. - To teach our community and peers about Asian American identities and interrogate what it means to be Asian American - To ask where do we fit into the greater picture of people of color? - To create a safe space to have uncomfortable discussions that encourage people to question their biases and grow - To create a safe and radical community for Asian Americans on campus; cultivate a sense of unity among different Asian American ethnicities - To learn from and stand in solidarity with other marginalized communities on campus in the fight against marginalization and towards liberation. This includes being staunchly against but not limited to, transphobia, queerphobia, sexism, racism, anti-Blackness, capitalism, imperialism, colonialism, ableism, Zionism, caste discrimination, religious discrimination, colorism, classism, xenophobia, and any other oppressive systems - To empower our own community and others

groups.name: GW Beach Volleyball Club
groups.category: Undergrad / Grad, Recreation / Social / General Interest
groups.description: GW Beach Volleyball Club addresses a clear gap at GW: there is no organized outlet for beach volleyball, a sport that is fundamentally distinct from indoor volleyball in its 2v2 format, outdoor sand play, and unique rules and skill set. This need was identified through direct conversations with students who wanted to play but had nowhere to do it. This interest is further evidenced by the fact that Lincoln Courts, a sand volleyball field, already exists nearby campus and is full every weekend without a student organization providing structure and activating it. The popularity of beach volleyball across DC, where recreational leagues and courts are widespread, reflects strong existing demand among young adults in this community. By forming this Club, GW students gain a welcoming, no-tryout, co-ed, athletic community which connects GW to the broader DC beach volleyball scene through interclub and eventually intercollegiate competition, and gives students a consistent outdoor community to be part of outside the classroom. GW Beach Volleyball Club is a community for anyone who loves the game or just wants to try it. We play beach volleyball, and that means something specific: 2v2 on sand, outdoors at Lincoln Courts, with its own rules, its own skills, and its own culture that's completely different from indoor club volleyball. Whether you've never touched a volleyball or you've been playing for years, you're welcome here. No tryouts, no pressure, just good competition and good people. We keep things flexible. You don't need to make every practice or every game, show up when you can, have fun, and meet people. Life gets busy and we get that, so there's no expectation that you're at every single session. That said, if you want to go all in, there's plenty of opportunity for that too and we love the people who do. DC has a legitimate beach volleyball scene and we want GW to have a real presence in it. Whether that's local scrimmages, organized DC games, or eventually traveling to tournaments against other schools, there's a path for you here regardless of how serious you want to take it. Beyond just playing, we're building something bigger. A tight knit group of people who genuinely enjoy spending time together on and off the sand. This club is new and growing fast, which means there's real room to shape what it becomes. Come for the volleyball, stay for the people. All skill levels, all backgrounds, all welcome. Just bring the energy and we'll handle the rest. Short-term goals for GW Beach Volleyball Club are to successfully recruit and retain a core membership of at least 15 to 20 active players in the first semester, establish a consistent weekly practice schedule at Lincoln Courts, and participate in at least one interclub beach volleyball competition in the DC area within the first academic year. These will be accomplished through active recruitment at student involvement fairs and on GW Engage, consistent weekly outdoor practices organized by the Vice President, and outreach to existing DC recreational beach volleyball leagues to identify competition opportunities. Long-term goals are to grow the Club's membership and competitive presence to the point of regularly competing against other beach volleyball clubs, establish GW as a recognized name in the DC beach volleyball community, and build a self-sustaining organization with strong year-over-year leadership continuity. These will be accomplished by developing a structured season calendar that balances casual social play with organized competition, building relationships with DC-area beach volleyball organizations and other university clubs, hosting open campus events to grow visibility and recruit new members each semester, and maintaining a strong officer transition process each spring so institutional knowledge carries forward as founding members graduate. The Club also plans to host internal 2v2 tournaments each semester as a low-barrier entry point for new members and a way to build community and competitive experience simultaneously.

Through intentional practices, meaningful programs, and collaborative leadership, we cultivate a culture where every Revolutionary feels valued, respected, and empowered. groups.name: Radiation Oncology Student Interest Group
groups.description: Radiation Oncology has continued to be a rapidly evolving field over the last several decades, driven by advancements in technology and oncology to support the clinical management of cancer. Despite these developments, the field has experienced a decline in the number of U.S. medical students pursuing radiation oncology residency. Survey-based studies have demonstrated that many medical students have limited awareness of the specialty and its career opportunities. The mission of the Radiation Oncology Student Interest Group (RadOncSIG) is to increase awareness and understanding of radiation oncology during the transformative medical school years. While GW already has an established Oncology Student Interest Group (ASCO-OSIG), RadOncSIG provides a distinct focus on radiation oncology as a specialty. Unlike many oncology subspecialties which are pursued through fellowship after residency, radiation oncology is a direct five-year residency following medical school (one year of general clinical work in an accredited internal medicine, family practice, surgery, pediatrics, or transitional year program, followed by four years of radiation oncology-specific training). Successfully pursuing this highly specialized and competitive field often requires early exposure to radiation oncology, meaningful specialty-specific clinical experiences, research, mentorship, and letters of recommendation. These opportunities are particularly important for students at GW, where there is currently no active radiation oncology residency program. RadOncSIG aims to bridge this gap by providing students with structured exposure to the field, connecting them with mentors and creating opportunities to develop the knowledge, experiences, and professional relationships necessary to explore and pursue residency and subsequent future career in radiation oncology. - Build professional and academic connections with practicing radiation oncology physicians in the Washington DC area and nationally, former GW SMHS students who are currently in radiation oncology residency, other current radiation oncology residents at highly competitive programs, and current GW SMHS students who are interested in radiation oncology - Understand the pathway to pursuing radiation oncology residency - Opportunities to join active research projects to strengthen application to radiation oncology residency - Advance knowledge about oncology, tumor biology, and molecular therapies, to support the clinical management of cancer We hope to encourage a diverse group of students to pursue radiation oncology residency to positively expand the population of residents, faculty members, and program directors, ultimately providing more culturally competent care to traditionally underserved populations.
groups.keywords: Radiation Oncology Student Interest Group RadOncSIG

groups.name: Sikh Initiative for Knowledge and Health
groups.description: The Sikh Initiative for Knowledge and Health (SIKH) at GW SMHS exists because we have found that the gurudwara (Sikh Temple), not the hospital waiting room, is where trust already lives for many Sikh and South Asian families, and that medicine should meet people there instead of waiting for them to find their way in. SIKH hopes to build a future where preventive care is simply part of gurudwara life, and where the next generation of physicians learns that good medicine starts with showing up where people already are. Joining this club puts you in direct contact with patients who often fall through the cracks of the healthcare systemâspecifically South Asian community members dealing with diabetes, heart disease, and other chronic conditions. You'll work in a small, hands-on clinic setting alongside other health professionals, which requires real conversations with patients, not just observing from the sidelines. You'll learn how to help someone navigate care when they potentially don't have insurance, don't speak English fluently, or don't know where to start, and how to navigate both their health and the broader system going forward. It's a chance to work with patients that the system tends to overlook, and start implementing the skills of cultural humility, patient navigation, plain-language communication outside of the classroom. SIKH works to close the gap between this community and the care it deserves, a gap shaped as much by language, trust, and unfamiliarity as by access alone. We aim to meet people in a way that respects how they actually live: the food they eat, the language they speak most comfortably, the role faith plays in their daily life, and the habits passed down through family. We want health information to travel the way trust does: through relationships, community elders, and repeated presence, as opposed to one-time outreach. We aim to strengthen the informal support networks that already exist within the gurudwara community, so that health becomes something neighbors look out for in each other, not something handled alone. We aim to support those who fall outside the reach of the traditional healthcare system by insurance status, immigration status, language, or simply unfamiliarity with how to navigate care.

groups.name: The George Washington University Bands
groups.description: GW Bands is an inclusive instrumental music organization at the George Washington University dedicated to producing quality musical performances, promoting school spirit, fostering strong friendships, and serving the community. GW Bands consists of three instrumental ensembles: Wind Ensemble, Symphonic Band, and the Foghorns Pep Band. All three ensembles rehearse twice a week on Tuesdays and Thursdays during the school year. The two concert bands, Wind Ensemble and Symphonic Band, make up the University Band class and perform at least one concert a semester. The Foghorns Pep Band performs at every home women's and men's basketball game as well at various events around campus throughout the year. In addition to playing music, we love to socialize and have fun together! University Band: GW Bands is the home of the Wind Ensemble and Symphonic Band, auditioned concert band ensembles in the George Washington Universityâs Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. Both ensembles rehearse on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The ensembles perform classic, contemporary and newly composed wind music with on-campus performances in the Fall and Spring. Membership in both groups is open to students from all schools and departments at GW and requires instructor approval via audition. Anyone who auditions for University Band is automatically welcomed into Symphonic Band; auditions are for seat placement and acceptance into Wind Ensemble. If accepted into Wind Ensemble, a student can choose to play in one or both ensembles. Auditions are held at the beginning of the Fall semester as well as at the beginning of the Spring semester and and on a case by case basis for anyone who joins throughout the year. Wind Ensemble meets Tuesdays and Thursdays from 3:45 - 5:00 PM ET. Symphonic Band meets Tuesdays and Thursdays from 5:10 - 6:25 PM ET. Foghorns Pep Band: The Foghorns Pep Band is a student organization that works with the Music Department and Athletics to put on a variety of performances around campus. We are an enthusiastic, passionate group of musicians who perform pop hits, classic rock favorites, and other modern songs to pump up our teams and energize GW fans. As the university's pep band, the Foghorns is the soundtrack to all men's and women's home basketball games. We can also be seen performing at various events and spots on campus, from performing in Kogan Plaza to get students excited for a big game to playing a fight song by the hippo to welcome newly accepted students to campus. The Foghorns also perform at the A-10 conference and other national tournaments during March Madness! The Foghorns are open to all GW students, but members must also participate in at least one of the University Band ensembles. As an added bonus, Foghorn members receive an award added to their financial aid for their participation. This award increases with each year you participate in The Foghorns. Foghorns meets every Tuesday and Thursday night from 7:10-8:10 PM ET. Being a part of our two concert bands, Symphonic Band and Wind Ensemble, and/or the Foghorns Pep Band is an incredible way to make friends, memories, and music. You DO NOT need to own an instrument to participate in or audition for Band. No one will be excluded from participating in band due to financial or any other barriers. We would absolutely love to have you!! If you are interested in joining GW Bands, please reach out to band@gwu.edu or request to join here.

groups.name: Young Americans for Freedom

groups.description: Young Americans for Freedom (YAF) was founded on September 11, 1960, by William F. Buckley Jr. in his childhood home in Sharon, Connecticut. The signing of the Sharon Statement, which, in 400 words, is described as the seminal document in the establishment of the modern conservative movement. During the 1960s and 1970s, YAF was instrumental in the campaigns for Goldwater and Reaganâs bid for the Republican nomination for the presidency, where the latter served as YAFâs honorary chairman from 1965 until his passing in 2004. Since its founding, YAF has been responsible for the creation of many influential political groups, from ACU, CPAC, and the National Journalism Center. YAF at GWU was founded in 2006 by Sergio Gor, and we continue to strive to be the intellectual hub for conservatism on campus. We welcome any ideas that people may hold and encourage them to share and develop them through productive collaboration and conversation with their peers. We are also active in campus culture and events. We are most well-known for hosting guest speakers such as Steve Forbes, Michael Knowles, Ben Shapiro, Senator Rand Paul, and many more on campus. In addition, we also hold panels and debates for students to discuss and share their beliefs in an intellectual setting. Every semester, we hold numerous retreats and conferences locally and nationally for GW students to attend, where they can hear and meet some of the most influential voices in American politics. We create a community to meet new friends, get involved, hear speakers, and share ideas that are united by values, not party politics. Young Americans for Freedom is part of the larger Young Americaâs Foundation. It is a 501(c)(3) Non-Profit organization and does not endorse or participate in any political campaigns.

events.title: Roommate & Suitemate Success Series: Understanding Roommate & Suitemate Conflict and Conflict & Personal Styles
events.location: Eckles Auditorium MVC, 2100 Foxhall Road NW, Washington, DC 20007
events.description: Living with a roommate is an opportunity to build communication, compromise, and community skills that make shared living more successful. Join us to learn practical strategies for communicating your needs, navigating disagreements, understanding different conflict styles, and creating a positive living environment. Through interactive activities and real-life scenarios, you’ll gain the tools to build a respectful, supportive, and successful roommate relationship. Workshop 2: Mount Vernon Campus Across three interactive sessions, you'll explore: Session 1: Understanding Roommate & Suitemate Conflict and Conflict & Personal Styles (October 19th) Session 2: Communication, Listening & De-escalation (October 26th) Session 3: Problem-Solving, Compromise & Roommate Scenarios (November 2nd) This session is number 1 of 3, offered twice during the fall semester. If you register for the first session, please plan to attend all three sessions. Can't make all three sessions on one campus? That's okay! You can mix and match between the two workshops on Foggy Bottom and Mount Vernon to complete all three sessions. We hope you'll join us for the Roommate & Suitemate Success Series and invest in making your shared space a place where everyone can thrive!

events.title: 100% Triumph GWU "The Upper Room" Study Hall
events.description: Upper Room Study Hall is a space to study with purpose, discipline, and faith because “faith without works is dead” (James 2:17). Rooted in the understanding that diligence honors God, we gather to steward our time well, sharpen our focus, and support one another in both academics and accountability. This is not just about productivity, it is showing up consistently, doing the work, and trusting that God blesses what we faithfully commit to Him. Come ready to lock in, stay disciplined, and be reminded that your obedience in the small things is part of your greater calling.
